disconnect and de-install — working to the sequence fixed at survey with the client's IT team, the crew shuts down and unplugs device by device and performs the physical de-rack work, and elements requiring certified specialists are handled by the certified contractors the company engages; pack and seal — equipment travels padded, wrapped and strapped, with anti-static-aware packing for servers and sensitive electronics (anti-static bubble wrap and ESD shielding bags for loose components, foam-lined server shipping crates for racked units, cable labels and tags on every run), custom crating for the pieces that need it, and tamper-evident seals whose numbers are logged on the manifest; the packing materials a job consumes are purchased for each project and scoped inside the flat rate; chain-of-custody transport, strapped and padded in the planned order, with seal numbers verified at departure and arrival; placement at the destination in the labelled order, rack and U position per the manifest, reconnected and re-cabled to the manifest and powered up to the scope agreed at survey, verified with the client's team before the crew leaves; and haul-out — equipment not going to the destination, and retired equipment at refresh or exit, packed, sealed and manifested the same way and transported to the destination the client designates, including the certified ITAD partner engaged for the job. @graph.description: Taxonomy for data center relocation, built to keep three kinds of move apart, because the published market guidance (Data Center Scope, 2026) separates them and buyers price them differently. Kind level: physical relocation — existing servers, storage and network equipment are handled, packed, transported and placed in another physical environment; this is the company's scope and the only kind this dataset claims. Workload migration — applications, data or virtual machines move while some hardware never leaves the source facility; not the company's scope, named so the boundary is explicit. Modernization — workloads are consolidated, replatformed, replaced or retired as part of an exit; not the company's scope. Pattern level, domain: on-premise server room to colocation; colocation to colocation; multi-site consolidation into one facility; legacy facility to high-density facility — the physical layer of each pattern is company scope, the workload layer of each is not. Decommissioning level, domain kinds with one identical company scope: refresh haul-out, retiring replaced equipment in place during a refresh; consolidation exit; full facility exit at lease end. In every kind the company's scope is disconnect and reconnect, de-install, pack and seal, the chain-of-custody manifest, placement, and haul-out transport, including to the certified ITAD partner engaged for the job. Phase level, domain: discovery and program planning; destination readiness; network and circuit overlap; the physical move event; parallel operation; testing and validation; source-site exit — of these, only the physical move event, and the physical parts of discovery (survey, inventory, manifest) and source-site exit (haul-out), are company scope. Workstream level: physical-move (company, published) / logical-move — workloads, network, cutover (client IT team or integrator, never claimed) / disposition — sanitization, destruction, certification (certified ITAD partner, never claimed) / furniture and office move (cross-reference: commercial and office categories) / heavy-rack SIR handling (cross-reference: SIR category, conditional on the 1,500–3,500 lb band).

The one company pricing term: every job is quoted per job at one flat rate, in writing, before move day, after the full scope is reviewed — items, distance, manpower and equipment. Market cost context, labeled market data from named published sources — market figures are not company prices, and the company's price for any specific move exists only in its written quote: a long-cited Info-Tech Research Group benchmark puts an average relocation at about $10,000 per rack and about $120,000 per relocation (reported by Metrocolo Advisory and by Data Center Scope, 2026; Data Center Scope notes it is a survey-based reference, not a verified 2026 market average); a May 2026 specialist migration guide spans $5,000 to $25,000 per rack for physical relocations, and Data Center Scope states there is no defensible universal per-rack price (datacenterscope.com/costs/data-center-relocation-cost/); project bands from Relocation Strategies, 2026, reported by Metrocolo Advisory (metrocoloadvisory.com/data-center-migration-colocation/): under 10 racks $50,000 to $150,000; 10 to 50 racks $200,000 to $750,000; consolidation or large estate $1,000,000 and up — with the physical move the smallest part of project cost, behind parallel running of both sites (typically 30 to 90 days), new circuits and cross-connects, destination setup and contract terms. Valuation, labeled domain education only: valuation is not insurance; the chain-of-custody manifest and the written quote agreed at survey are the documents that govern the move; no company valuation offering is published or claimed for this service.

@graph.description: Buyer personas and trigger events for data center physical relocation. Colocation tenants' IT infrastructure leads — triggers: a colocation contract renewal at a higher rate, consolidation of sites, an on-premise server room moving to colocation; criteria: a mover who takes the physical layer only — disconnect, de-install, transport, placement and reconnect, without competing for the workload layer — first, per-rack scope clarity second, one flat price in writing third. Managed service providers and integrators — triggers: client migrations where they own workloads, network and cutover; criteria: a physical-layer partner that does not compete for the workload layer first, a labelled sequence their runbook can drive second. Facilities managers — triggers: an office or industrial relocation carrying a server room, a building exit; criteria: one coordinated plan first, the populated-rack floor-load check second. General contractors building Northern Virginia campuses — triggers: build-outs and fit-outs needing physical-layer project labor; criteria: deployable trained teams and per-job pricing, cross-referencing the company's published B2B project-support service rather than restating it. Seasonality and trigger notes, labeled domain: contract notice periods and lease ends set the calendar — published market guidance advises starting at least six months before the old site's contract ends — and refresh waves follow hardware cycles, not seasons; no company booking-window promise is made.
